theme: The bridal song and its Messianic echo
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 45. You read this psalm in Unit 9, with attention to the king. Today read it again, this time paying special attention to the bride in verses 10 to 17 and to how the psalm echoes the Song of Solomon.
settingTheScene: Psalm 45 is a royal wedding song, and in Unit 9 (Day 290) you read it as a portrait of the Davidic king. Now it appears at the close of the wisdom books, right after the Song of Solomon. The two works belong together. Both celebrate a royal wedding and a bridegroom’s love, and both have been read by the church as a picture of Christ and his people. This time, look at the bride.
observation: “My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king” (v. 1).
“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever” (v. 6).
“At your right hand stands the queen in gold of Ophir” (v. 9).
“Hear, O daughter, consider, and incline your ear: forget your people and your father’s house” (v. 10).
“and the king will desire your beauty. Since he is your lord, bow to him” (v. 11).
“All glorious is the princess in her chamber, with robes interwoven with gold” (v. 13).
“With joy and gladness they are led along as they enter the palace of the king” (v. 15).
“I will cause your name to be remembered in all generations; therefore nations will praise you forever and ever” (v. 17).
interpretation:
In Unit 9 the focus was on the king: his majesty, his righteousness, and his eternal throne. Here the focus shifts to the bride. She is told to forget her people and her father’s house. A wedding means leaving one family to join another. It echoes Genesis 2:24: “A man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife.” She is called to a new loyalty. The call is not a loss but a gain, because “the king will desire your beauty.” Her beauty is a gift of his love.

The bride is clothed in splendor. She stands at the king’s right hand in gold. She is led to the king in embroidered garments, with companions, with joy and gladness. The picture is not of a servant but of a queen. In the Song of Solomon, we saw the same mutual delight of the bridegroom and bride. In both texts, love is a covenant that transforms and glorifies.

Reading with the Song in mind, we notice how both works use the language of royalty and beauty to speak of love. The bridegroom is a king, and the bride is a queen. The ordinary becomes extraordinary. A wedding is a picture of how God loves his people.

The psalm closes with a promise concerning the king’s name: “Nations will praise you forever.” The love story of the king extends to the nations. What began as a royal wedding becomes a universal blessing.

Read with the whole Bible, the psalm points to Christ the King and his bride the church, a love that began in a promise and ends in a wedding feast. The wisdom books end with love, which is the end of wisdom: knowing and being known by God.
connection: Ephesians 5:25-27 says that Christ loved the church and gave himself for her, “that he might present the church to himself in splendor.” Revelation 19:7-8 shows the bride arrayed in fine linen, bright and pure. Revelation 21:2 pictures the New Jerusalem “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.” Hebrews 1:8-9 quotes verses 6 and 7 of this psalm of the Son. Jesus is the Bridegroom (Mark 2:19-20).
application:
Read verse 10 as a call to give your first loyalty to Christ. What does “forget your father’s house” mean for you?

Thank God that the Bridegroom desires his people.

Think about how the church is being prepared for the wedding. How can you take part?
prayerPrompts: Tell God what fills your heart as you think of the King and his bride.
Ask him to teach you to give Christ your first loyalty.
Ask him to prepare his church for his coming.
